paragraphs: Training decision trees across several machines can become expensive because the machines must exchange information about candidate splits. PV-Tree addresses this communication problem by using votes to narrow the set of attributes worth examining in detail. The training data are partitioned across machines, each of which evaluates attributes using its own portion of the data.

In each iteration, every machine selects its top k attributes and sends their indices to a server. The server uses majority voting to choose the globally top 2k candidates. Only then do the machines transmit detailed histograms for those candidates, allowing the algorithm to select an informative attribute and its split point.

This staged exchange makes communication cost independent of the total number of attributes. The theoretical analysis shows that the best attribute can be found with high probability, supporting a near-optimal decision tree. Experiments on real datasets report a substantially better accuracy–efficiency tradeoff than existing parallel tree algorithms.
neurips-2016-a-communication-efficient-p.tldr: PV-Tree reduces distributed decision-tree communication by voting on candidate attributes before exchanging detailed split information.

paragraphs: MARMANN is an active learning algorithm that builds a nearest-neighbor classifier from a pool of examples. Instead of receiving labels without choosing which examples matter, it selectively requests labels. It works in general metric spaces, so its formulation relies on distances between examples rather than requiring a particular coordinate representation.

The method combines a generalized sample compression scheme with a procedure for choosing a model while using few labels. These components connect the task of retaining a useful representation of the sample with the task of deciding where additional labeling is worthwhile. The resulting classifier remains a nearest-neighbor rule.

The paper provides prediction-error guarantees that depend on the sample's noisy-margin properties, making the guarantee sensitive to separation and noise in the input. Those guarantees are competitive with earlier passive learners. At comparable guaranteed error, the authors prove significantly lower label complexity than any passive learner, establishing a theoretical benefit from choosing which labels to request.
neurips-2016-active-nearest-neighbor-lea.tldr: MARMANN selectively requests labels to obtain nearest-neighbor prediction guarantees with significantly lower label complexity than comparable passive learners.

paragraphs: Second-order online learning uses more information about the learning problem than a single update direction, but maintaining and processing that information can be computationally expensive. This paper introduces Sketched Online Newton, or SON, to make that approach more practical. The algorithm modifies Online Newton Step using sketching techniques.

A sketch provides a compact representation of the information used by the update. In SON, the resulting running time scales linearly with the data dimension and the sketch size. This connects the amount of retained information directly to computation, addressing the cost that can make second-order methods difficult to apply to high-dimensional examples.

The authors also develop sparse versions of sketching methods, including Oja's rule, so computation scales linearly with feature sparsity. Alongside these computational changes, SON has substantially improved regret guarantees for ill-conditioned data. The contribution therefore combines a learning guarantee for difficult data geometry with implementations designed to exploit both compact summaries and sparse inputs.
neurips-2016-efficient-second-order-onli.tldr: Sketched Online Newton combines improved regret guarantees for ill-conditioned data with efficient updates based on compact, potentially sparse sketches.

paragraphs: Planning can become difficult even when an environment has only a modest number of states. For people and animals, limited working memory and time pressure make this especially consequential. Hierarchical representations offer a possible solution by dividing an environment into modules, but that leaves a central question: which division makes planning efficient?

The paper develops a normative theory that answers this question through information-theoretic description length. It selects a partition that minimizes the average description length of planning in the environment. This objective balances two sources of complexity: planning between modules and planning inside each module. The preferred representation is the one that optimally trades off those costs under the proposed criterion.

The authors show that the resulting representations provide a common account of multiple behavioral and neural phenomena previously treated as unrelated. The significance is both computational and explanatory: a concrete efficiency principle determines the modules and connects their organization to patterns in behavior and neural representation.
neurips-2016-efficient-state-space-modul.tldr: The paper explains modular planning representations by minimizing the information needed to plan within and between modules.

paragraphs: This paper proposes website navigation as a benchmark that combines language understanding with sequential planning. An agent must follow hyperlinks to reach a page containing a query. Pages form the nodes of a directed graph, and hyperlinks form its edges. Because the environment is only partially observed, success requires making useful decisions from incomplete information.

The authors release WebNav, software that converts a website into this task, and construct WikiNav from English Wikipedia. They evaluate several neural-agent variants and report that the benchmark reflects advances in the models. This makes navigation a way to test how improvements in language-based reasoning translate into a sequence of actions.

They also extend WikiNav with Jeopardy! question–answer pairs and compare a recurrent neural agent with strong search systems based on inverted indexes. The trained agents outperform those search approaches in the reported evaluation. These findings support goal-driven navigation as a proxy for progress on tasks such as focused crawling and question answering.
neurips-2016-end-to-end-goal-driven-web-.tldr: WebNav turns websites into navigation benchmarks for evaluating agents that combine language understanding with planning.

paragraphs: This paper studies how signals move through deep neural networks with random weights. It combines Riemannian geometry, which describes curved spaces, with mean-field theory for high-dimensional chaos. The aim is to give mathematical meaning to the expressive power of depth by analyzing the geometry of the functions these networks compute.

The analysis reveals a phase transition. In the chaotic phase, the global curvature of the computed nonlinear functions grows exponentially with network depth, but not with width. The authors also prove that a generic class of these random functions cannot be computed efficiently by any shallow network. This extends the argument beyond demonstrations built around a single specially chosen function.

The framework further quantifies how deep networks can transform exponentially curved input manifolds into flat manifolds in hidden representations. Together, these results connect depth to both complicated function geometry and the ability to simplify geometric structure internally. The claims concern the analyzed random-network setting and its chaotic phase.
neurips-2016-exponential-expressivity-in.tldr: In a chaotic phase, random deep networks compute functions whose curvature grows exponentially with depth and that shallow networks cannot efficiently represent.

paragraphs: Large multichannel neural recordings need automated spike sorting that is accurate, fast, and economical to review manually. KiloSort addresses these requirements with an integrated framework that uses waveform templates during both spike detection and clustering. This gives the two stages a shared way to describe the recorded electrical signals.

The framework models voltage as a sum of template waveforms occurring at spike times. That additive representation allows it to identify and resolve overlapping spikes. KiloSort works on raw recordings instead of first compressing them with PCA, which the authors report supports more accurate waveform modeling. Batch-based optimization on GPUs reduces processing time.

Against an established sorting algorithm, KiloSort shows favorable performance with much shorter processing times. A subsequent merging step uses template continuity to reduce manual corrections further. The reported substantial reduction concerns the evaluated data and neurons with near-zero error rates. The findings support progress toward fully automated sorting, rather than establishing that manual review has already become unnecessary.
neurips-2016-fast-and-accurate-spike-sor.tldr: KiloSort uses raw-signal template matching and GPU optimization to sort neural spikes quickly while reducing manual curation.

paragraphs: Bayesian nonparametric models based on Dirichlet, gamma, and beta processes capture many useful aspects of data, but their ability to represent power-law behavior is limited. Stable, generalized gamma, and stable-beta processes offer alternatives for that purpose. Their statistical appeal, however, brings practical challenges when computing posterior inferences from data.

The paper introduces a family called independent, identically distributed finite-dimensional BFRY processes. The motivation parallels finite-dimensional versions of the Dirichlet process: develop a tractable construction that helps turn a useful prior model into workable inference algorithms. The authors position this family as a foundation for efficient methods, including variational Bayes, that can scale to massive datasets.

As an illustration, they construct a simple variational Bayes algorithm for mixture models based on a normalized stable process. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate its usefulness. The contribution is therefore both a new process construction and an example of how it can support practical inference for power-law modeling.
neurips-2016-finite-dimensional-bfry-pri.tldr: Finite-dimensional BFRY processes provide a foundation for scalable Bayesian inference in models designed to capture power-law behavior.

paragraphs: Factorization machines are supervised models that can use interactions between pairs of features even when the feature space is very large. Higher-order factorization machines extend that idea to combinations involving more features. The problem addressed here is how to train these richer models efficiently, rather than leaving their additional expressive capacity difficult to use.

The authors present generic training algorithms for factorization machines of arbitrary order, claiming the first efficient algorithms with that scope. Supporting arbitrary order means the contribution is not restricted to one particular size of feature combination. It provides a way to train the broader family of higher-order models.

The paper also introduces variants that share parameters, substantially reducing model size and prediction time while retaining similar accuracy. These variants address the practical cost of using a trained model as well as the cost of fitting it. Evaluations on four link-prediction tasks demonstrate the proposed approaches, connecting efficient higher-order training with compact prediction models.
neurips-2016-higher-order-factorization-.tldr: The paper introduces efficient training for arbitrary-order factorization machines and parameter-sharing variants that reduce model size and prediction time.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a very deep encoder–decoder network for restoring corrupted images, including denoising and super-resolution. It learns the mapping from degraded images to their originals end to end. Convolutional layers extract representations of image content while removing corruption, and deconvolutional layers reconstruct image details from those representations.

Its central design choice is to connect corresponding convolutional and deconvolutional layers through symmetric skip connections. These links serve two purposes. They give training signals a direct route back to lower layers, addressing vanishing gradients, and they carry image details forward to the reconstruction layers. The same connections therefore support both optimization and preservation of useful visual information.

The authors report faster convergence, a higher-quality local optimum, and improved restoration performance from this design. They also state that the network's capacity allows one model to handle different noise levels. Experiments show better performance than recent leading methods, supporting the combination of network depth with direct paths for gradients and image details.
neurips-2016-image-restoration-using-ver.tldr: Symmetric skip connections help a deep image-restoration network train more effectively and preserve details during reconstruction.

paragraphs: This paper addresses exploration in Markov decision processes using a probably approximately correct, or PAC, framework. Such a framework seeks guarantees about learning sufficiently good behavior with high probability. The authors introduce the median of means into a PAC exploration algorithm, presenting it as the first application of this estimation method in that setting.

The main result changes what the theoretical bounds depend on. Their dependence on the full range of possible value-function values is significantly reduced, while dependence on the variance of the Bellman operator is introduced. That variance can be much smaller, so the improvement is potentially substantial when the variability captured by this quantity is favorable.

The algorithm also extends the reach of PAC exploration guarantees to Markov decision processes with unbounded rewards, which the authors identify as a first. The contribution is therefore about both sharper dependence in the bounds and a broader reward setting. The abstract's potential advantage remains tied to the variance rather than asserting an unconditional improvement for every process.
neurips-2016-improving-pac-exploration-u.tldr: Using the median of means improves PAC exploration bounds through variance dependence and permits guarantees for MDPs with unbounded rewards.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn an optimal Bayesian-network structure while respecting background knowledge about ancestry. An ancestral constraint concerns whether one variable lies upstream of another through the network. Such requirements involve relationships across the structure, making them difficult to handle with learning tools that operate through decomposable scores.

The proposed approach uses a framework for optimal structure learning with non-decomposable scores. Within it, the authors exploit existing structure-learning oracles that accept decomposable scores and constraints. The key step is to infer decomposable constraints from the ancestral requirements and pass those usable constraints to the oracles. This lets locally organized tools contribute to solving a problem with global structural restrictions.

The empirical results show that this approach can be orders of magnitude more efficient than alternatives such as integer-linear-programming frameworks. The improvement is an observed possibility, not a universal runtime guarantee. Its practical significance is that background knowledge about ancestry can be incorporated while retaining the objective of optimal structure learning.
neurips-2016-learning-bayesian-networks-.tldr: The method turns implications of ancestral constraints into constraints existing Bayesian-network learning tools can use efficiently.

paragraphs: This paper develops an online dictionary-learning method for decomposing brain images into components that are both sparse and spatially structured. Sparsity means most entries in each component are zero. Spatial structure means the remaining pattern forms compact, piecewise-smooth regions, helping the decomposition describe recognizable brain structures instead of scattered activations.

The method combines an ℓ1 constraint, which imposes sparsity, with a Sobolev or Laplacian penalty that encourages spatial smoothness. Together, these restrictions shape the learned dictionary components into localized blobs. The approach extends an existing online dictionary-learning method, with an overall running-time cost reported as a factor of two or three.

Because learning is online, the algorithm retains the ability to scale to arbitrarily sized datasets. Experiments on brain data report structured, denoised components that are more interpretable and capture differences between subjects better than leading comparison models. These benefits appear across small, medium, and large data regimes, linking spatially meaningful components with scalable processing.
neurips-2016-learning-brain-regions-via-.tldr: Combining sparsity and spatial smoothness produces scalable brain-image decompositions with more interpretable, localized components.

paragraphs: The paper asks how convolutional neural networks can recognize new categories from only a few examples. Its approach adds an unsupervised meta-training stage that exposes multiple units in the network's upper layers to many unlabeled real-world images. This stage aims to make those units describe visual structure more broadly than a particular set of training categories.

The method encourages diverse low-density separators: boundaries that pass through sparsely populated parts of the unlabeled data. An unsupervised margin-maximization procedure jointly estimates compact, high-density regions and the separators between them. Learning these two aspects together provides a way to organize visual representations without requiring category labels for the additional images.

The resulting low-density-separator modules can be inserted into any or all upper layers of a standard CNN. The authors report significant improvements in scene classification, fine-grained recognition, and action recognition when training samples are scarce. These findings support unlabeled meta-training as a way to make upper-layer representations more useful for learning unfamiliar categories.
neurips-2016-learning-from-small-sample-.tldr: Unsupervised meta-training teaches CNN upper layers broader visual structure, improving recognition when labeled examples are scarce.

paragraphs: The paper compares an R-W learning model with a Bayesian approach in a visual-search task whose environmental volatility varies. The motivating distinction is between unpredictable randomness and changes in an underlying regularity. How a learner interprets that uncertainty can influence whether recent outcomes should cause substantial changes in behavior.

Both models reflected individuals' estimates of volatility, and the R-W learning rate strongly correlated with the Bayesian belief in stationarity across volatility conditions. In the low-volatility condition, the R-W learning rate correlated positively with lose-shift behavior, meaning switching after a loss, while its relationship with choice optimality had an inverted-U shape. Bayesian stationarity belief correlated positively with choice optimality, while its relationship with lose-shift behavior was inverted-U shaped.

Compared with expert learners, suboptimal learners who switched frequently after losses had significantly higher fitted R-W learning rates and lower Bayesian stationarity beliefs. These results show how the two modeling approaches connect different aspects of uncertainty estimation to behavior, with distinct relationships to switching and successful choices.
neurips-2016-learning-under-uncertainty-.tldr: R-W and Bayesian models both track perceived volatility but reveal different relationships between uncertainty estimates, switching after losses, and choice quality.

paragraphs: Many sparse-estimation algorithms repeatedly apply a linear filter followed by thresholding. Each iteration resembles a neural-network layer, so a sequence of iterations can be viewed as a deep network with shared, hand-designed weights. This paper asks whether learning those computations from ample training data can improve sparse estimation, with accuracy as its main focus.

The difficult setting involves dictionaries whose columns are highly coherent, as reflected in a large restricted-isometry constant. In such settings, many tractable iterative methods fail to find representations using the fewest nonzero coefficients. The authors present theoretical and empirical evidence that trained deep networks can recover minimum-ℓ0 representations in regimes where existing methods fail.

The resulting system can effectively learn new iterative sparse-estimation procedures. It is applied to photometric stereo, where sparse outliers interfere with estimating surface normals in a three-dimensional scene. The contribution establishes the potential of learned estimators in challenging sparse-recovery regimes, rather than claiming that every trained network always finds the sparsest representation.
neurips-2016-maximal-sparsity-with-deep-.tldr: Trained deep networks can recover maximally sparse representations in some regimes where conventional iterative methods fail.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo produces approximate posterior samples, but determining how closely those samples match the desired distribution is difficult. Black-box inference systems make this particularly important because their automation can conceal failures. This paper extends bidirectional Monte Carlo into a method for evaluating MCMC-based posterior inference.

On simulated data, the method runs annealed importance-sampling chains in both directions: from prior to posterior and from posterior to prior. These paired calculations provide an upper bound in expectation on the symmetrized KL divergence between the true posterior and the distribution of approximate samples. The result measures distributional discrepancy, with the expectation qualification forming part of the guarantee.

The authors integrate the method into WebPPL and Stan and validate it across several models and datasets. They also use it to examine how different model representations affect inference in those systems. This illustrates how a diagnostic can inform algorithm design by evaluating the consequences of modeling choices, alongside its role in assessing sample reliability.
neurips-2016-measuring-the-reliability-o.tldr: Bidirectional Monte Carlo evaluates MCMC inference on simulated data by bounding posterior-sample discrepancy in expectation.

paragraphs: Online convex optimization includes problems that are much easier than the general case. MetaGrad aims to exploit that favorable structure automatically, without manually choosing a learning rate for each problem class. Its scope includes strongly convex and exp-concave objectives, along with some stochastic and non-stochastic objectives that have no curvature.

The algorithm considers multiple learning rates simultaneously. A tilted exponential-weights master algorithm weights them according to their observed performance on the data. Unlike the earlier methods with provable regret guarantees discussed in the abstract, its rates need not decrease monotonically, and their weighting is not based on tuning a theoretical regret bound.

This adaptation supports fast rates across a broader collection of problems. One example is logarithmic regret for unregularized hinge loss when the data follow a favorable probability distribution, despite that loss having no curvature. The condition on the distribution matters: the result shows that useful structure beyond curvature can enable fast learning, rather than guaranteeing logarithmic regret for every hinge-loss sequence.
neurips-2016-metagrad-multiple-learning-.tldr: MetaGrad weights multiple learning rates by empirical performance to adapt automatically to a broad range of easier online-learning problems.

paragraphs: Multi-view anomaly detection looks for instances whose different views are inconsistent with one another. The paper models that inconsistency through hidden, or latent, vectors. For a non-anomalous instance, all views are assumed to originate from one shared vector, expressing the idea that they describe the same underlying instance coherently.

An anomalous instance is instead assumed to require multiple latent vectors, with different views generated from different vectors. The model uses Dirichlet-process priors to infer how many latent vectors each instance needs. That inferred multiplicity produces an anomaly score, connecting unusual cross-view disagreement to the model's explanation of how the observations were generated.

The authors interpret the approach as a robust extension of probabilistic canonical correlation analysis for noisy multi-view data. They develop Bayesian inference procedures based on stochastic expectation maximization and demonstrate effectiveness in detecting multi-view anomalies. The central contribution is a probabilistic account of disagreement among views, with the single-vector versus multiple-vector assumption providing the basis for detection.
neurips-2016-multi-view-anomaly-detectio.tldr: The model detects inconsistent views by inferring whether an instance requires one shared latent explanation or several different ones.

paragraphs: Comparing structured objects often begins by comparing their parts. Convolution kernels sum similarities across all pairs of parts, whereas assignment kernels choose an optimal one-to-one matching. A matching can offer a more appropriate notion of similarity, but optimal assignments generally produce indefinite functions, complicating their use in methods that require positive-semidefinite kernels.

The paper characterizes a class of kernels for comparing individual parts that guarantees a positive-semidefinite optimal-assignment kernel. These base kernels induce hierarchical structures. Using those hierarchies, the assignment similarity can be computed through histogram intersection in linear time. The result connects a validity guarantee with an efficient computation for the identified class.

The authors apply this construction to graphs by developing a Weisfeiler–Lehman optimal-assignment kernel. On widely used graph-classification benchmarks, it provides high accuracy and improves over the original Weisfeiler–Lehman kernel. The findings show how carefully choosing the part-comparison kernel can make assignment-based similarity both compatible with kernel methods and useful for classification.
neurips-2016-on-valid-optimal-assignment.tldr: A characterized class of base kernels makes optimal-assignment similarities valid and efficient, enabling improved graph classification.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why depth can be computationally useful and how much depth a network should have. Rather than analyzing an unrestricted neural network, it studies a simple model with clustered, noisy inputs and a simple learning rule. That controlled setting makes it possible to derive mathematical descriptions of signal propagation.

The authors obtain recursion relations that describe how signals change as they pass through successive layers. They then define performance measures and analyze those equations to determine how network depth affects performance. This approach ties architectural choices to the evolution of signals inside the model, rather than treating the number of layers as an unexplained design parameter.

The analysis shows that these model networks have optimal depths. The authors also explore how the preferred architecture changes with system parameters. The result therefore supports a parameter-dependent balance in network depth within the studied setting. It contributes to theoretical understanding of deep computation while also relating to interest in hierarchical sensory processing in the cortex.
neurips-2016-optimal-architectures-in-a-.tldr: An analytically tractable model shows that deep networks can have optimal depths that depend on the system's parameters.

paragraphs: Principal components analysis provides an optimal linear encoding of data, but sparse encoders offer a different advantage: features that depend on fewer inputs can be easier to interpret and may generalize better. This paper asks how much approximation quality must be traded away when the encoder is required to have a specified level of sparsity.

The authors formulate two linked questions. First, what is the best approximation to PCA available at that sparsity level? Second, can an efficient algorithm attain the optimal combinatorial tradeoff? These questions connect the quality of a sparse representation with the difficulty of finding it, rather than evaluating sparsity only as a descriptive property of a learned model.

The paper answers them by providing what it identifies as the first polynomial-time algorithms for constructing optimal sparse linear autoencoders. It also demonstrates the algorithms on real data. The contribution establishes efficient access to the stated optimal sparsity–approximation tradeoff, while the motivation of improved generalization remains a potential benefit of sparse features.
neurips-2016-optimal-sparse-linear-encod.tldr: The paper provides polynomial-time algorithms that attain the optimal tradeoff between sparse linear encoding and approximation to PCA.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover depth from a single photograph taken in an unconstrained setting. Its focus is depth perception in ordinary images rather than a narrowly controlled collection. To support that task, the authors introduce Depth in the Wild, a dataset whose images carry relative-depth annotations between randomly chosen pairs of points.

These annotations describe how depths compare at two locations rather than directly supplying a complete metric-depth map. The paper also introduces an algorithm that learns to estimate metric depth using this relative information. This connects a comparatively limited form of supervision with a richer prediction target: the model uses pairwise depth relationships to help learn depth estimates.

The authors report that the algorithm is simpler and performs better than the state of the art they compare against. Experiments combine the new relative-depth annotations with existing RGB-D data and show significant improvements in single-image depth perception in the wild. The result supports the usefulness of both the added supervision and the proposed learning approach.
neurips-2016-single-image-depth-percepti.tldr: Depth in the Wild and a new learning algorithm use relative-depth annotations to improve depth estimation from unconstrained photographs.

paragraphs: The paper considers how to find a low-rank approximation of the matrix product AᵀB while reading each input matrix only once. A straightforward approach would compress A and B separately into sketches and then apply PCA to those summaries. The proposed algorithm keeps extra information during the same pass to improve the approximation.

That additional information includes summaries such as row and column norms. Rather than treating the sketches as the only available description of the inputs, the method uses these summaries alongside them. The central idea is that retaining a little more information about the original matrices can make the eventual product approximation more informative without requiring another pass.

The main theoretical result gives a spectral-norm guarantee comparable to existing two-pass methods. An Apache Spark implementation also shows better computational and statistical performance on the evaluated synthetic and real-world datasets. Together, the results support single-pass processing as a way to obtain a useful product approximation while preserving a strong error guarantee.
neurips-2016-single-pass-pca-of-matrix-p.tldr: Extra matrix summaries improve single-pass sketches of AᵀB, yielding an error guarantee comparable to two-pass methods.

paragraphs: Word mover's distance compares documents by solving an optimal-transport problem between their embedded words. This turns word-level semantic representations into a document-level distance, but the original distance is unsupervised. The paper introduces Supervised Word Mover's Distance to let available labels influence which semantic distinctions matter when comparing documents.

The method learns a linear transformation of the word-embedding space together with weights tailored to individual words. Training minimizes stochastic leave-one-out nearest-neighbor classification error at the document level. In this way, supervision about documents changes both the geometry used to compare their words and the contribution of particular words to the learned distance.

The authors evaluate the resulting metric on eight real-world text-classification tasks. S-WMD consistently outperforms almost all of the 26 competitive baselines included in the evaluation. The finding supports adapting the underlying word comparisons to a supervised task, while preserving the optimal-transport approach that connects those comparisons to distances between whole documents.
neurips-2016-supervised-word-mover-s-dis.tldr: Supervised Word Mover's Distance learns word-space transformations and word-specific weights to improve document comparisons for classification.
